 Disney, Mark Goldbridge and more sports: What next for The Overlap’s podcast empire?
 The Overlap has transformed from a creative outlet for pundits into a multimillion-dollar content machine. Chief executive Scott Melvin explains how the company has evolved, where the content space is going, and why fan channels are no longer a laughing matter.
 10 November 2026 
 Steve McCaskill 
 News 
 The Overlap
 SHARE THIS ARTICLE 
 The Overlap started because Gary Neville “had an itch to scratch”, according to the company’s chief executive Scott Melvin. 
 Former Manchester United and England full back and current Sky Sports pundit Neville began interviewing leading sporting figures in 2021 before launching ‘Stick to Football’, a fortnightly discussion show with other ex-players and pundits, two years later.
 On the face of it, The Overlap was nothing remarkable – something Melvin freely admits. But viewers enjoyed the content, recognised the quality of the lineup, and embraced the format.
 The Overlap was in the right place at the right time to capture demand for digital-first, ‘always-on’ conversations about sport. Now, five years on, what was once a side venture is a multimillion-dollar business in its own right, positioning itself at the forefront of a new wave of creator-led media companies that are transcending their medium, signing huge deals with major streaming services and increasingly setting the media agenda.
 “[The Overlap] was almost an accident,” Melvin tells the Sportel sports business conference in Monaco. “Stick to Football was a bit of an experiment. It’s not a revolutionary idea: let’s get five people around a table and talk about football. You know, it’s not rocket science.
 “But then very quickly we realised that something special was happening. And then we realised, actually, this is not just a hustle, this is a business, and we started seeing monetisation kick in and realised this needs a lot more attention than we’re probably giving it.”
 Owning the conversation
 Comparisons with Goalhanger’s The Rest Is Football have been inevitable. Both shows are fronted by a former player turned broadcaster called Gary, and both lean heavily on high-profile talent from established broadcasters. Whereas Goalhanger co-founder Gary Lineker enlisted the support of his then Match of the Day colleagues Alan Shearer and Micah Richards, Neville is supported by his fellow Sky and ITV pundits Roy Keane, Ian Wright and Jill Scott.
 Lineker has since parted ways with the BBC , but it is telling that so many of the country’s leading soccer voices have been able to cultivate their own brands to the point that they no longer depend on their primary employers to reach fans. The Rest is Football and The Overlap also have streaming deals with Netflix and Disney+, respectively, meaning they now have global scale and, at least in the cases of Lineker and Neville, even greater wealth.
 In January, The Overlap was purchased by Global , one of the largest commercial radio operators in the UK and Europe, in a deal designed to bolster the company’s push into digital audio and video content.
 Global created a dedicated sports division last year and saw The Overlap’s audience and talent roster as valuable assets. The Overlap generated 2.2 billion views across all platforms and 38 million monthly views on YouTube last year, illustrating that its panellists are capable of attracting a wide church of listeners and viewers, not just digitally engaged younger audiences.
 Melvin attributes the success of Stick to Football to the fact that it isn’t overproduced and that its talent is given time and freedom to discuss what they want. Stick to Football is released fortnightly, with one topical show released in the morning followed by a more evergreen episode with a guest interview later in the afternoon.
 “Live [sport] is the most important thing – it drives everything we do,” Melvin explains. “But rights are prohibitively expensive for any creator and there’s only one or two channels that can afford the Premier League . So, if you can’t own the rights, own the conversation. Most teams only play once a week so there are more than 150 hours when they’re not playing. That’s a big opportunity so how do you try and own that conversation?”

 ‘We needed to be more reactive’
 The Overlap’s existing cadence works perfectly as appointment viewing for fans who want to hear the panel’s opinions on the biggest topics of the moment. Indeed, there was great anticipation about what Neville and Keane would say about Manchester United after their 3-0 home defeat against Bournemouth last month, despite both appearing on Sky Sports’ live coverage of the match.
 But it doesn’t work as well when a major news story breaks in between recordings. Melvin says any outlet or creator seeking to dominate the conversation in between live events needs to be more agile and flexible.
 “Last November, Ruben Amorim was sacked by Man United on a Monday morning,” Melvin recalls. “We didn’t talk about it for ten days and we were sat there saying, ‘How can we be a home for football conversation when we don’t discuss a Man United manager getting sacked for ten days?’”
 “People were [giving us stick] online for not talking about [the sacking]. But we have a schedule and to try and get the five people we have on the panel together at a day’s notice is impossible. So, we just had to suck it up and wait.
 “It was not ideal. So we launched Overlap Daily so we can be kind of always on. It’s only one hour a day; it’s not a full five-hour slot. But we knew we needed to be more reactive, and the World Cup proved that beyond any doubt: the appetite for football is 24/7. It’s 365 days a year. There’s always something to go on. So, it’s a case of trying to be as reactive and as relevant as possible.”
 Going for Goldbridge
 However, launching a more regular podcast in a crowded marketplace populated by traditional media giants and established creators is no easy task, even for a well-known brand like The Overlap.
 Melvin’s solution was to work with another creator with a reputation for volume and an existing but complementary audience that could provide a foundation not just for a daily soccer podcast, but also a future club network.
 Mark Goldbridge, real name Brent Di Cesare, was once ridiculed for his enthusiastic and arguably performatively angry watchalongs on his streaming channels. But he had also established himself as one of the leading lights of the fan-led content creation movement, growing a following of millions on his United Stand channel before expanding into general soccer with ‘That’s Football’.
 Accordingly, Global acquired both for a reported seven-figure sum , transforming ‘That’s Football’ into ‘The Overlap Daily’ and adding more journalists and ex-professionals to join Goldbridge. A similar approach has been adapted for ‘The United Stand’, with Wayne Rooney among several big names to join the show – something that would have been unthinkable just a few years ago.
 “We knew we wanted to try and move into club-specific [content] and it would have been [the] easiest thing in the world for us to start a Man United channel,” says Melvin.
 “But it’s taken Mark 12 years to build up to 2.5 million subscribers. It’s taken us five [years] to get to 1.8 [million]. So, we could start a Man United channel and be at two million subs in ten years, or we partner with Mark, and instantly you’ve got 2.5 million Man United fans, and then another 1.5 [million] on [That’s Football]. So, for us, it was a shortcut, but we knew he had a super-engaged community there already.
 “I spent 18 years at Sky Sports. We were there at the same time, and we used to laugh at fan channels, because it was just angry, shouty, reactive. The joke’s on us now, because they are killing it, both from a credibility point of view and financially from brand partnerships. It’s definitely no laughing matter.
 This model could be replicated in the future with other channels as The Overlap seeks to build out a network of club-specific shows. After a successful shift to cricket, expansion into other sports is also on the cards.
 View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Overlap (@wearetheoverlap) 
 Mickey mouse punditry
 It’s not just creators who want to control the conversation. Global streamers are keen to bring sports content to their platforms, making them relevant for fans without having to acquire expensive and fragmented live rights. This opened the door for a distribution deal with Disney+, bringing The Overlap’s portfolio to a worldwide, mainstream audience.
 However, YouTube remains an important route to market. Video accounts for 80 per cent of The Overlap’s consumption and, although audio distribution remains significant, the company is investing significantly to increase that proportion so it can secure more lucrative brand partnerships and commercial revenues.
 “Brand and advertising money is all shifting towards YouTube … and this is just the beginning,” Melvin says. “It’s only going one way and I think you’re going to see more and more rights holders and athletes come onto the platform.”
 But partnerships are just part of the equation. Popular podcasts with a loyal fanbase are increasingly embracing memberships and subscriptions that offer additional content, access and community features to super fans willing to engage more.
 The Overlap believes its talent and content mix are significant assets when it comes to diversifying its revenue streams, with fan loyalty a crucial factor in overcoming the challenges of subscription fatigue.
 “The thing with subscriptions is price is different to value,” Melvin explains. “If a subscription is value for money people will come, and we are always conscious that you don’t want to be seen as taking liberties with your audience.
 “Our subscription is the price of a coffee. It’s UK£4.99 – that’s not even a pint in London. So, we think it’s good value, and I think if the value is right, you’ve got a chance.
 “One thing you can’t do is take the piss out of your audience, because they’ll know.”
